Montréal-Nord est en général présenté da: Montréal-Nord is generally portrayed in the media through the lens of violence. But behind the gunshots and the gangs, there is a disadvantaged neighbourhood, a void, a glaring lack of services. Residents told us about it. They are fed up with repeating themselves. They feel abandoned.
« Montréal-Nord, c’est un bouquet de fle: “Montréal-Nord is a bouquet of flowers. It's multicoloured, with many kinds of flowers,” says resident El Yakout Choukrat in the garden of the building where she has lived since 2003. What drives her is the neighbourhood's diversity and community spirit. “People help each other out. If someone loses a family member, we go see them to comfort them. If someone needs money, or if someone is sick, we pool our money. We do really wonderful things,” explains the mother of two teenagers. She says she is tired of talking about the lack of resources in the neighbourhood and the violence that comes with it. “The situation is well known. The violence in Montréal-Nord exists. Everyone knows about it. We talk, but nothing changes. We wonder why we have to keep repeating the same thing,” confides Ms. Choukrat, who is a member of the Montréal-Nord mothers' collective against violence, set up after the murder of Abderrahmane Hadj-Ahmed, who was shot on rue Lapierre, very close to her home. The mothers' collective has taken several actions to counter the violence. In March, they launched a petition calling for more resources for community organizations and for young people. The provincial Minister of Labour, Employment and Social Solidarity, Jean Boulet, responded to the mothers' request in a letter, a copy of which La Converse has obtained. In it, he states that the request is rejected and that “the resources are there” to develop youth employability. But nothing is moving forward, says Ms. Choukrat. “We feel neglected, abandoned,” she tells us with emotion. On August 19, the collective once again spoke out to denounce the institutions' inaction in the face of the violence and the underfunding that afflicts the neighbourhood. “Young people are falling. They started with delinquency and moved on to crime. But what alternative to the street were they given?” she asked during the press conference in front of the crowd gathered in the garden. “We cry hot tears, and we break out in cold sweats for ourselves and for our children. We've had enough of hearing gunshots; I don't want to see the image of a young person lying on the ground anymore. I want action,” she exclaims. Maria Di Angelo lives a few steps from El Yakout Choukrat. The local resident is also involved in the mothers' collective. She explains that parents lack the resources to help their children. It is hard, then, for the neighbourhood's young people to dream of a promising future. “The way things are here, there's no future for our children, there's only the street,” she laments. “There's drugs, prostitution, there's too much violence and we have to do something to change that. Kids can't see beyond that if it's all they're exposed to, if there's nothing for them to go further. To go further, how are we going to do it?” she asks.

Quelques coins de rue plus loin, on se r: A few street corners away, we find ourselves in the offices of the Café-Jeunesse Multiculturel. “Montréal-Nord isn't problems, it's a territory where people live, and there are people who live very well in Montréal-Nord,” says Slim Hammami, the centre's coordinator, from behind a desk. He is keen to point out that the neighbourhood is a very pleasant place to live, like any other borough. “Every family has worries. We're all afraid our kids will do something stupid, that they'll turn to drugs or delinquency. Now, as for the gunshots, that involves a small minority of young people who act on it,” he adds. He explains that his mission involves, among other things, correcting the falsehoods circulating about the neighbourhood. For Mr. Hammami, an entire population of young people is being left behind in the neighbourhood. Marginalized youth who haven't found their place in organizations and institutions, and who turn to “subsistence income” because they lack opportunities and prospects. “In 20 years, or 30 years, or 40 years, we haven't been able to change the game; that's a real question,” says the youth worker. Le Café-Jeunesse Multiculturel déploie d: The Café-Jeunesse Multiculturel deploys street workers who help and support young people who are going through difficulties or who have broken with their living environment. There have only been three of them, sometimes two, for the entire borough for more than 10 years. Faced with governments' lack of investment, the organization has had to turn to philanthropic foundations for support in order to keep paying its current street workers and hire more. It is a situation that several other community players denounce. The organization's coordinator thinks we need to stop dehumanizing the neighbourhood's marginalized youth. “I often say as a joke: ‘The marginalized youth of Montréal-Nord, they're the not-so-pretty, they're the ones we don't want to see.’ We don't want to see them, we don't want to give them an existence, we don't want to let them have a second chance, we don't want to let ourselves offer them certain opportunities.” The focus is on children, and the older ones are neglected. “It's easier with the little ones, they're more malleable, they listen. Working with guys coming out of prison, who have a difficult past, yes, that's hard. But it's work that's necessary if we want to restore a certain balance. We have to take care of these young people. As long as we don't make the ‘not-so-pretty’ pretty, the situation won't change.” While several residents of rue Lapierre complain about the young people who gather in the area, Mr. Hammami believes that's not the problem. “The real story is that marginalized youth have no place to gather,” he explains. Painting a picture of the situation, he says that when young people first hang out in the park, they are urged to go elsewhere. The police stepped in, applying pressure. The neighbourhood's youth then headed to rue Pierre, which automatically became the meeting place. “They stayed there for a few years. Then they said they didn't want them anymore, so they left.” Rue Pascal became the young people's spot, before they were forced to move again and ended up at the Espace Lapierre. “We've had the same problem for 20 years, but nobody wants to fix it. We've never asked ourselves: ‘But why are these people there? What are they doing, what do they want?’” laments Mr. Hammami.
Ted Rutland, professeur à l’Université C: Ted Rutland, a professor at Concordia University and a specialist in racial profiling, sees a vicious circle in this police repression. “There are people who grow up in a world where it's very hard to feel valued and to earn a living in the legal market. Some turn to illegal activities. This crime and violence lead to more police repression, and the cycle repeats,” he explains. It is a phenomenon that has persisted for years in Montréal-Nord. The researcher believes that the gun violence plaguing the neighbourhood stems from a social problem and that policing can only be a short-term solution. He advocates long-term investments in social programs and community groups in order to tackle the issue. “The problem is that in neighbourhoods like Montréal-Nord, the long term never arrives,” says the professor. The organization Hoodstock echoes this. General coordinator Cassandra Exumé would like decision-makers to understand that the violence is the result of neglect that has lasted more than 10 years. She lays out the demands of the neighbourhood's residents and community players. “Let's tackle economic insecurity, let's care about young people, let's give them a living space like we see elsewhere,” she lists. “We're a few minutes from neighbourhoods where there's a bit more love and care – we simply want the same thing. This youth is just as great, and it too can have an influence on the metropolis, the province and the country.” The organization's co-founder, Nargess Mustapha, agrees. “Enough with the stopgap solutions,” she said at a press conference.

Les voitures du Service de police de la: Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) cars are omnipresent on rue Lapierre, where young people gather. In the middle of the afternoon, they pass more than four times in an hour as we talk with Paroles d’excluEs mobilization officer Nomez Najac. “The only service that's super high-performing in the neighbourhood is the SPVM. They have equipment, they have a presence; I don't even know how many of them there are,” he observes of the police presence in north Montréal. He points to a glaring lack of community resources to help young people. “If we put more money into everything upstream of delinquency, the number of people who fall into it would go down, because people would turn to other services that exist,” believes the social worker. He would like these youth services to be as visible as the police presence. “We shouldn't be surprised that so many people end up in the hands of the police, because it's the only service that exists,” he says. He believes that if we expect young people to follow a certain trajectory, it's a lost cause from the start. “It's like putting people in a maze – but we know they'll make their way through and always end up on the same route, because we don't give them the possibilities that would let them branch off to other places,” he sums up. What would he like to say to decision-makers? “Do they believe in these young people?” asks the mobilization officer. On that point, he thinks politicians' actions must speak louder than their words. “If they believe so, that change is possible, we'll see it in their actions too. If they don't believe it, it's because it's tied to a racist reading. It's that we don't believe in these young people because they're racialized,” he says.

Imane Salemi, Imene Souagui, Sedat Solak: Imane Salemi, Imene Souagui, Sedat Solak, Farhat Adoum and Revenel Geffrand are community facilitators at Un itinéraire pour tous, an organization that offers activities to young people in Montréal-Nord. They hope for better investment of resources. “I'd like governments to be present on the ground with us. Because I get the impression that they sometimes invest in useless things and forget the basics,” says Imene Souagui. It is a demand that also resonates in other disadvantaged neighbourhoods of Montréal. The Coalition Pozé, which brings together players and community workers from Black communities in different Montréal neighbourhoods, is calling for a $90 million investment for racialized Black youth in the city. At a press conference Thursday morning, the group asked mayoral candidates and elected officials to review the budget allocated to young Montrealers. The coalition wants a coherent strategy to reach young people in the neighbourhoods of north Montréal. Last September, the Quebec government launched Operation Centaure, the <l1>Quebec strategy to combat gun-related violence</l1>. With an investment of more than $90 million, the provincial government proposes to strengthen police forces to curb gun violence across Quebec, mainly in the greater Montréal region. But for the Coalition Pozé, the same amount should be invested to support racialized youth in disadvantaged neighbourhoods. “How is it that we can have $90 million for police resources, but getting $90 million for young people is so complicated?” says Pierreson Vaval, director of the community organization Équipe RDP, indignantly. He denounces the “scattershot investments” given to youth. “Our workers who have experience, who are able to work with young people, who have their trust – they're the ones who need to be there with them. And those workers, they need to be paid,” he adds, noting that there is an exodus of resources from the community sector. Mr. Vaval thinks we need to invest in the problem instead of dividing the issue up by neighbourhood. For him, there are too few organizations with the resources to work with young people who fall into delinquency or are at risk of doing so. “There are very few workers, and they don't have enough support. So it takes a massive and strategic investment,” proposes the coalition's spokesperson.
La députée du Parti libéral du Québec Pa: Quebec Liberal Party MNA Paule Robitaille asked for an initiative mandate on violence and mental health problems in Montréal-Nord to assess the needs of community services. Parliament refused the mandate on the grounds that it would carry out its own assessment and did not need to hold a consultation. Asked about it, the provincial government would only say that it was a parliamentary decision.
À Montréal-Nord, le taux de chômage des: In Montréal-Nord, the unemployment rate for young people aged 29 and under is about twice as high as in Quebec as a whole. More than half of Montréal-Nord families with a child under five are low-income.
D’après une étude publiée en 2019 par le: According to a study published in 2019 by the Centre des jeunes L’Escale, the neighbourhood receives more than seven times less money from the Ministry of Health and Social Services (MSSS) than the Ville-Marie borough. The study also found that only one other Montréal borough receives less MSSS funding per organization than Montréal-Nord.
En 2020-2021, le MSSS a accordé une somm: In 2020-2021, the MSSS granted $2 million to 41 community organizations to prevent youth delinquency and crime through the Proceeds of Crime Sharing Funding Program (PFIPPC). Barely $42,224 of that sum went to Montréal-Nord this year. That is the funding received by the Café-Jeunesse for street workers.
Dans le cadre des programmes de financem: Under its crime prevention funding programs, the MSSS invested $266,537 in Montréal-Nord in 2020-2021.
Dans le cadre du Programme de prévention: Under the Program for the Prevention of Delinquency through Sports, Arts and Culture, the MSSS granted $224,313 in 2020-2021 to Montréal-Nord to support three projects.
